A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Default MoE and retain the same central framework. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated material.

before.justification: v1 reports original language-model pretraining results, benchmark evaluations, throughput measurements, and architecture and EMA ablations.

after.justification: v3 reports original pretraining and benchmark results, additional routing-method comparisons, and empirical analyses of gradients, expert specialization, and load balance.

M1.justification: The core sparse computation and EMA-based dense-router-gradient approximation remain. v3 Sections 4.3 and A.4 introduce router-score-weighted accumulation into the default-vector update and explicitly describe it as the final method. This refines v1's unweighted averaging to reduce sensitivity to the EMA decay parameter.

E1.justification: FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu were already used in v1. v3 adds BoolQ, PubMedQA, and SciQ to benchmark evaluation, and Appendix B.1 adds routing-specialization evaluations across ArXiv, GitHub, Pile-CC, PubMed Central, and StackExchange domains. These additions substantially broaden the evaluated data and task coverage.

E2.justification: TopK and SparseMixer comparisons are retained. v3 Section 4.4 additionally evaluates ReMoE, reporting failure to recover from training divergence, and Loss-Free Balancing with a tuned bias-update coefficient. Both were only discussed or cited in v1, so the evaluated routing alternatives expand substantially.

E3.justification: The main benchmark comparison changes from 320B-token 8c1 models to 160B-token 8c1 and 32c4 models. New protocols include a 1/64-sparsity configuration and varying K from 1 to 7 against a fully activated gradient reference. Benchmark random-reference values and improvement-over-random normalization also change. Global auxiliary-loss reduction was already documented in v1.

E4.justification: v3 adds scored-versus-unscored EMA sensitivity tests, a more extreme sparsity ablation, and extensive analyses of router entropy, dense-gradient similarity, default-vector similarity, domain specialization, load balance, and expert coactivation. These test mechanisms and potential side effects beyond v1's architecture and EMA ablations, many of which remain in the appendix.

E5.justification: v1's benchmark table lacks uncertainty estimates. v3 Table 2 adds standard errors throughout the benchmark comparisons; the checklist attributes them to lm-eval-harness and states that pretraining is typically conducted once per configuration. Section 4.6 also adds throughput variability estimates. This substantially expands uncertainty reporting without establishing additional training runs.

E6.justification: v1 Table 1 reports a 2.8% average benchmark advantage; v3 Table 2 reports 2.1% for 8c1 and 0.3% for 32c4, with some task-level losses. These are different-budget, different-coverage comparisons, not same-setting performance changes. New findings include Loss-Free Balancing perplexity of 24.22 versus Default MoE's 23.48, ReMoE nonconvergence, and gradient-similarity results. The throughput table's numerical results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equations 1–11 retain the router-gradient construction, gradient-error expressions, expectation argument, and EMA formulation. The added weighted-update variant and empirical explanations are not accompanied by new formal assumptions, mathematical derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains improved MoE training through approximate dense router gradients with minimal overhead. v3's introduction explicitly scopes its benchmark evidence to approximately 2B-parameter models trained on 160B tokens, and its conclusion newly claims that additional hyperparameter tuning is unnecessary.

C2.justification: v3 Sections 4.4–5 develop explanations connecting router entropy, default-vector similarity, gradient approximation, and training stability, and attribute competing methods' weaker results to globally reduced auxiliary loss. New Appendix A.1 qualifies industrial applicability of dropless MoEs and identifies untested reasoning, specialized coding/math, and finetuning settings. v1 lacks this substantive mechanism and limitations discussion.

D1.justification: Most architecture, optimizer, batch-size, and auxiliary-loss details are relocated to Appendix A.2. v3 adds explicit active-parameter counts, identifies Liger as the Triton-kernel source, discloses 64-GPU AWS execution, and replaces the GitHub pointer with anonymous code and configuration links. The previously printed minimum learning rate is omitted. These are limited documentation and access-information changes.

R1.justification: v3 adds Qiu et al. (2025) to contextualize stronger globally balanced baselines and Hsu et al. (2024) for Liger kernels, while removing several background references, including Dai et al. (2024) and Kaplan et al. (2020). The comparison framing changes, but the core positioning as a lightweight improvement to sparse MoE routing remains.

P1.justification: v3 condenses the introduction, moves implementation details into the appendix, separates routing comparisons and empirical analysis into dedicated subsections, and rewrites the discussion around a mechanistic explanation. The appendices are reorganized around limitations, experimental details, ablations, and detailed analyses, followed by a checklist. This is substantial narrative restructuring.

P2.justification: The opening benchmark bar chart is removed, the benchmark table is transposed and expanded, and an active-parameter table is added. Separate ablation plots are consolidated into Figure 2, while several retained curves move to the appendix. New heatmaps, domain-routing charts, and polar gradient-similarity plots substantially change the visual presentation.

improvement.justification: v3 substantially strengthens evidence for the central mechanism: Section 4.5 and Appendix B directly test dense-gradient approximation and examine routing behavior, which v1 did not. Additional evaluated competitors, the weighted-update ablation, benchmark standard errors, and explicit limitations improve scrutiny and transparency. Reporting remains imperfect: the weighted final method is not integrated into Equation 10, and retained approximately 320B-token material is not clearly reconciled with the revised 160B-token benchmarks. These weaknesses temper, but do not outweigh, the substantial gains in empirical support.
